subtype: Giving up a seat or space [Actor]
passage:
So Avni, you asked why I stood up on the metro that day. Honestly, I hadn’t planned anything. I’m Ujjwal, and I was just tired, scrolling on my phone. Then I saw an elderly lady near the door holding the pole with both hands as the train jerked.
Six or seven of us were sitting, and everyone was looking at their screens or the floor. I stood and said, “Please, have this seat.” She smiled and said thank you. A college kid in the corner suddenly stood up for the man next to her, too.
Nobody clapped, and I didn’t want that. My legs ached a bit. But I felt lighter for the rest of the ride.

qa.q: Where did Ujjwal give up the seat?
qa.a: Ujjwal gave up the seat on the metro.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal feel afterwards, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt lighter. Despite aching legs, Ujjwal said that feeling lasted for the rest of the ride, and did not want clapping or praise.

qa.q: What led Ujjwal to stand up at that moment?
qa.a: Ujjwal noticed the elderly lady holding the pole with both hands as the train jerked. Seeing that need was enough, with no plan behind it.

qa.q: What might the college kid in the corner have been thinking before standing?
qa.a: The college kid may have hesitated like the others, then felt nudged by Ujjwal's example. Standing up for the man next to the lady suggests the kid noticed someone else's need too.

grounding: Shows a young adult giving up a metro seat to an elderly person out of awareness of others, with no wish for praise.

subtype: Giving up a seat or space [Actor]
passage:
I saw it on the 8:10 local train, Thursday. The compartment was jammed, and most people were sitting with their eyes half shut. Sumit, a man from my building, was standing near the door with his laptop bag. When a pregnant woman stepped in, he looked around for a moment. Nobody moved. Then he said quietly to a seated teenager, “Could she sit here?” and stepped aside himself.
The teenager blinked and jumped up. The woman thanked Sumit, and he only nodded. He looked a little tired, but he didn’t seem to want anything back.
I’m Pooja, and I remember thinking I should have been the one to offer.

qa.q: Which train was Pooja on at the time of this scene?
qa.a: Pooja was on the 8:10 local train on Thursday.

qa.q: What does Sumit's quiet nod suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests Sumit did not want thanks or attention. He may have felt tired, but he seemed satisfied simply to have made room for the woman.

qa.q: What choice did Sumit make when nobody moved?
qa.a: Sumit spoke up quietly to the seated teenager and asked whether the woman could sit there. He gave way himself and did not wait for someone else to act.

qa.q: How might the pregnant woman have felt stepping into the packed compartment?
qa.a: She was probably relieved to be offered a seat and also a bit uneasy at standing among so many people, though the passage only shows her thanking Sumit.

grounding: Shows an observer seeing a young adult make space for a pregnant woman on a train quietly and without wanting praise.

subtype: Giving up a seat or space [Actor]
passage:
'Finally, seats!' Kalyani dropped onto the bus bench. 'My feet are dead.'
Keerthana sat beside her. 'Same. Ten hours standing at the store.'
At the next stop a woman climbed in, one hand on her belly, the other clutching a steel tiffin.
Keerthana stood up. 'Akka, sit here.'
'No, no, you're tired too,' the woman said.
'You're carrying two people. I'm carrying one.'
The woman laughed and sat. An old man nearby said, 'Good girl, very nice.'
Keerthana shrugged and held the overhead bar.
Kalyani whispered, 'You didn't have to.'
'I know.' Keerthana swayed with the bus. 'My sister had a baby last year. She said nobody ever gave her a seat.'
'Now I feel guilty.'
'Don't. Just next time.'

qa.q: How long had Keerthana been standing at the store?
qa.a: Ten hours.

qa.q: Why did Keerthana give up the seat despite being tired?
qa.a: She felt empathy and concern, remembering her sister saying nobody ever gave her a seat when pregnant.

qa.q: How did Keerthana handle the old man's praise?
qa.a: She shrugged and held the bar, needing no praise for a small act.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling after Keerthana's explanation?
qa.a: Kalyani felt a little guilty for staying seated, and Keerthana gently let it go with 'Just next time'.

grounding: A tired young woman gives her bus seat to a pregnant woman out of awareness and needs no praise for it.

subtype: Giving up a seat or space [Actor]
passage: I used to pretend to be asleep on the metro. Headphones in, eyes shut, so I'd never have to decide whether someone needed my seat. Then one evening an old man with a walking stick stood swaying in front of me for three stations. My colleague Zeenat, standing near the door, was watching. I pretended not to notice. When he nearly fell at a curve, a schoolgirl caught his arm. I felt terrible. The next day I kept my eyes open. When an elderly woman got on with shopping bags, I stood up before thinking about it and said, 'Please, sit.' She smiled and sat. Nobody clapped. Zeenat just nodded at me. I'm Varun, and now I keep my eyes open on the metro.

qa.q: For how many stations did the old man stand in front of Varun?
qa.a: Three stations.

qa.q: How did Varun feel when the schoolgirl caught the old man's arm?
qa.a: Varun felt terrible, guilty and ashamed for pretending not to notice.

qa.q: What small habit did Varun change?
qa.a: Keeping eyes open on the metro, so Varun notices who needs a seat and offers it straight away.

qa.q: What might Zeenat's nod mean?
qa.a: Zeenat seems to have noticed the change and quietly approves, without making a fuss.

grounding: A young adult moves from avoiding notice to giving up a seat for an elderly person, without needing praise.

subtype: Giving up a seat or space [Actor]
passage: Waiting-room note, eye clinic, Monday. Busy morning; every chair taken and fourteen patients standing. Madhav, the young man who brings his grandfather every week, gave up his chair when Minakshi, clearly pregnant and holding a toddler, came in. He did it without a word, just stood and gestured. When the lady beside him said, 'Such a good boy,' he looked embarrassed and moved to the window. His grandfather patted his hand. A few minutes later, two more people stood up for elderly patients. I have asked the office for six more chairs and a priority seating sign by the entrance.

qa.q: How many patients were standing?
qa.a: Fourteen.

qa.q: What does Madhav moving to the window after the praise suggest?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed by the attention; he gave the seat out of awareness, not for praise.

qa.q: What did the note-writer do next, and why?
qa.a: Asked for six more chairs and a priority seating sign, so giving way is easier and doesn't depend on one person.

qa.q: How might Minakshi feel being offered the chair?
qa.a: Relieved and grateful, since she was pregnant and holding a toddler in a full room.

grounding: A clinic note records a young man quietly giving his seat to a pregnant woman, uncomfortable with praise.

subtype: Giving up a seat or space [Actor]
passage:
Thursday, 9:40 p.m.
Crowded metro home, standing room only. I finally got a seat at the interchange and sank into it like a king. Two stops later a woman got on with one hand on her belly and a heavy office bag, clearly pregnant. The man next to me closed his eyes. The college boys opposite stared hard at their phones. I stood up and said, "Please sit." She said, "Thank you, I'm Ayesha, but I'll be fine for two stops." I said, "So will I." She sat. That was it. Nobody clapped. Honestly, my feet ached for the next forty minutes, and I was a bit grumpy about it. But I kept thinking of my sister last year, standing on a bus in her eighth month because nobody looked up. I'd rather be the one who looks up.
Pankaj

qa.q: How long did Pankaj's feet ache after standing up?
qa.a: For the next forty minutes.

qa.q: How did Pankaj feel after giving up the seat?
qa.a: Pankaj felt a bit grumpy about aching feet but settled about the choice, remembering the sister and not needing anyone to clap.

qa.q: What could other passengers learn from Pankaj?
qa.a: Looking up from the phone and offering a seat quietly takes a moment, and it matters without any applause.

qa.q: What might the ride have been like for Ayesha if no one had stood?
qa.a: She would have stood with a heavy bag while pregnant, probably tired and uncomfortable, like Pankaj's sister last year.

grounding: Pankaj's diary shows a young adult giving up a metro seat to a pregnant woman out of awareness, with no need for praise.
